title: The home shrine
hookLine: an image, a candle, incense, a flower, water: a small corner
last: NAMO TASSA — A BOW IN A WORD.

cards: Every home already has shrines; they just don't get called that. The fridge door with the kids' drawings and the save-the-date. The shelf with a grandparent's photo and a candle that's never lit.
The nightstand where the phone sleeps, glowing, the first thing you touch every morning. People arrange these small altars without thinking, and then the altars arrange them.
Buddhist homes, from Sri Lanka to Japan to a studio apartment in Denver, often keep one corner arranged on purpose. Today: the home shrine.

teach.h: AN IMAGE, A CANDLE, INCENSE, A FLOWER, WATER.
teach.b: A home shrine can be tiny: a shelf, the top of a bookcase, a corner of a table. The traditional pieces are simple. An image of the Buddha, often seated in meditation.
A candle or small lamp. Incense. A flower.
Clean water in a small bowl or cup. The flower, the candle and the incense get their own days later this week, so today is about the space itself. A few customs come up often.

teach.h: HIGH, CLEAN, NEVER ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: The image goes somewhere high and clean, often at or above head height when you're seated, never on the floor, never in a bathroom or next to shoes. It's kept dusted. Fresh flowers replace wilted ones.
Some people put the shrine where they'll see it first in the morning. Traditions differ in the details.

teach.h: SEVEN BOWLS; A CABINET; A SHELF.
teach.b: In Tibetan homes you may see a row of seven small bowls of water, filled each morning and emptied in the evening.
In Japan, families may keep a butsudan, a wooden cabinet that holds a Buddha image along with the names of family members who have died.
In Theravada homes, the shrine may hold a small Buddha image, a photo of a respected teacher, and the day's offerings. What's the image for? Buddhist teachers say it isn't a god and it isn't magic.
It's a reminder: of the Buddha, of what's possible, of the practice you meant to do today.
The shrine turns a corner of the house into a place where the mind remembers what it's for. It doesn't need to be expensive or beautiful. It needs to be clean, cared for, and yours.

how: Many Buddhist households keep a small shrine with a Buddha image placed high and clean, and offer a candle, incense, flowers and water there each day; Japanese families often keep a butsudan cabinet that also honors ancestors.

games.q: match the tradition to its home shrine.
p: high and clean, never on the floor

s: a home shrine has to be large and expensive
it can be a single shelf; it needs to be clean and cared for.
many Japanese families' butsudan also honors family members who have died
it holds a Buddha image and the names of the family's dead.
Buddhists describe the image as a god living in the house
they describe it as a reminder of the Buddha and the practice.

games.q: you've been given a small Buddha image. where do you put it?
o: on the floor by the door.
on a clean shelf, at or above head height when you're seated.
in the bathroom, where it's quiet.
games.why: custom puts the image somewhere high and clean, never on the floor or in the bathroom, often where you'll see it first in the morning.

practice: In your mind, walk through your home and look for a small space that could be a quiet corner: a shelf, a windowsill, the top of a dresser, somewhere clean and a little above your head when you sit.
Picture it cleared, and picture what might go there: an image, a stone, a candle, a cup of water, whatever means something to you. Rest with the breath in that corner.

wordCard.voice: Butsudan. A household altar cabinet: the home shrine, small, clean and high, with an image, a candle, incense, a flower and water.
